ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Although a cross-dock / e-commerce overseas fulfillment undertaking is typically not itself a reporting entity under the AML/CFT Act 2009, all New Zealand banks and non-bank payment providers (including Airwallex, local ACH operators and correspondent banks) will contractually require the company to evidence beneficial ownership, PEP-free status and sanctions clearance during onboarding. Mandatory screening protocol therefore comprises: customer due diligence under the AML/CFT Act 2009 and Regulations 2011, including identification and verification of the ultimate beneficial owner at the 25% ownership or control threshold; compulsory screening of directors, shareholders, authorised signatories and beneficial owners against the New Zealand Consolidated Sanctions List and UN Security Council sanctions (Sanctions Act 2019), the NZ terrorist designations list (Terrorism Suppression Act 2002), and domestic and foreign Politically Exposed Persons registers, including family members and close associates of PEPs as defined in regulation 24 of the AML/CFT Regulations 2011; enhanced due diligence for high-risk jurisdictions; OFAC SDN screening is not domestically mandated but is contractually mandatory for US-dollar payment rails and is therefore included; all records retained for at least 5 years.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office - Companies Register (online portal: https://companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz, integrated with the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) system through https://www.nzbn.govt.nz)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Company names must be in Latin script (A-Z letters, numerals and permitted punctuation), may be in English or te reo Maori, and must not be likely to mislead or be otherwise contrary to sections 21-22 of the Companies Act 1993. No transliteration doctrine applies; no local-character translation is required because New Zealand is an English-language jurisdiction. Each name must be distinguishable from existing registered names and reserved names and must not be identical or confusingly similar to a name already on the Companies Register.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: A name reservation is held for 20 working days from the date of reservation and lapses automatically thereafter; the Companies Office does not administratively extend reservations, and the applicant must re-file the reservation if incorporation is not completed within the window. If the Registrar refuses to register the proposed name, the grounds are given in writing under section 25 of the Companies Act 1993. The applicant may submit a written reconsideration request to the Registrar of Companies, including a statutory declaration or evidence that restricted-word consent has been obtained from the relevant regulator (Reserve Bank of New Zealand, Financial Markets Authority, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, or Tertiary Education Commission). If reconsideration is declined, the applicant may apply to the High Court of New Zealand for judicial review of Registrar decisions under the Judicature Amendment Act 1972 and may apply for interim relief; no separate statutory administrative appeal body exists for name refusals.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Partially permissible. Section 194 of the Companies Act 1993 requires the registered office to be a physical street address in New Zealand at which service of documents may be effected and at which the company's records are available or accessible. A pure mail-forwarding virtual office or a post office box address alone is not permitted. A virtual office product is acceptable only if the provider offers a genuine physical New Zealand street address, can accept service of process, provides space for statutory record inspection and is staffed during ordinary business hours. The company will in practice use the licensed registered agent's premises.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low - estimated below 5% annual probability for a standard low-risk overseas cross-dock / e-commerce order fulfillment company whose registered office is the address of a licensed registered agent. Nonetheless, the Registrar of Companies, the Financial Markets Authority and NZ Police financial intelligence functions retain statutory powers to conduct unannounced inspections, demand production of the share register, beneficial ownership data and corporate records, and verify commercial substance under the Companies Act 1993 and the AML/CFT Act 2009.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand), sections 10 and 12 (formation and name restrictions), sections 14-15 (registration and certificate of incorporation), sections 87-90 (share allotment and share registers), sections 122-124 (share capital), sections 145-153 (directors and appointment of officers), and section 189 (registered office and address for service). The Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 does not apply because the company is a private exempt company.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (Ngā Kaihautū Kamupene o Aotearoa), a business unit of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), operating the New Zealand Companies Register and the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) register.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Form NZCN1, formally titled Application for Registration of a Company (Incorporation Application), submitted electronically through the Companies Office online portal, resulting in the issuance of a Certificate of Registration and the automatic allocation of a New Zealand Business Number (NZBN).
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital applies under the Companies Act 1993; a company limited by shares may issue shares of no par value with a nil or nominal paid-up amount. No escrow, trust account, or stated capital deposit is required at incorporation, and 100% non-resident ownership is permitted without exchange control approval.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLUTIONS OF THE FIRST BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF THE COMPANY ADOPTED BY UNANIMOUS WRITTEN CONSENT PURSUANT TO THE COMPANIES ACT 1993, SECTIONS 145 AND 189. (1) SUBSCRIPTION AND ALLOTMENT OF SHARES: RESOLVED that the offer and subscription for 1,000 ordinary shares of no par value at an issue price of NZ$1.00 per share set out in the subscriptions accompanying this resolution be and is hereby ratified, approved, and adopted, and the directors be and are hereby authorized to allot and issue such shares, to enter the allotment in the share register in accordance with sections 87 and 90 of the Companies Act 1993, and to execute and deliver share certificates to the subscribers. (2) REGISTERED OFFICE AND ADDRESS FOR SERVICE: RESOLVED that the registered office of the Company shall be situated at the place specified in the Company Register in New Zealand and that the Board appoints the corporate services provider identified in the incorporation application as the agent of the Company for service of process and as the address for service in New Zealand under section 189. (3) APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS: RESOLVED that the persons named in the register of directors be and are hereby appointed as the first directors of the Company, each having filed a signed consent to act, and that the Board hereby appoints a Chief Executive Officer for Cross-Border Fulfillment, a Company Secretary, and an Authorized Representative for New Zealand operations, each with delegated authority to execute leases, bank mandates, and logistics contracts in the ordinary course of the third-party logistics cross-dock business. (4) BANKING AND GENERAL AUTHORITY: RESOLVED that the directors be and are hereby authorized to open and operate corporate bank accounts with licensed New Zealand banks and approved electronic payment platforms (including local ACH, Airwallex, and SWIFT wire facilities) and to appoint such sub-managers as may be required to conduct the e-commerce fulfillment hub business in accordance with the company strategy.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Company Name Availability Search and NZBN Pre-Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Companies Register online portal (www.companiesoffice.govt.nz) and the NZBN Register
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a name availability search for the proposed company name and at least one alternative. Verify compliance with section 22 of the Companies Act 1993, which prohibits names that are identical or almost identical to an existing name, that include restricted words without consent, or that are likely to mislead. Optionally reserve the approved name online for up to 20 working days before submission of the incorporation application.
required_dossiers: Proposed company name and three alternative names
Full legal names, residential addresses, and dates of birth of all proposed directors
Full legal names and shareholding details of all proposed shareholders
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the proposed name is refused, the applicant may file a written submission with the Companies Office demonstrating distinctive character and absence of misleading effect under section 22(3). Where immediate cure is unlikely, select an alternative name from the reserved list and restart the incorporation filing without incurring an additional statutory fee if filed within the same application session.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Shareholders and board of directors, with concurrent filing obligations at the New Zealand Companies Office upon incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Determine whether to adopt the default constitution prescribed in the First Schedule of the Companies Act 1993 or to adopt a bespoke constitution addressing share class rights, cross-border management delegation, director indemnity, and dispute resolution. Draft and execute the constitution, obtain signed consents to act as directors, and prepare a shareholders agreement where multiple subscribers are present. The constitution becomes effective upon registration of the company.
required_dossiers: Constitution (if a bespoke constitution is adopted)
Consent to act as director for each proposed director
Shareholders agreement (optional but recommended for cross-border structures)
Certificate of identity for non-resident directors or shareholders
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a defect in the constitution is identified after registration, the board may convene a special shareholder meeting and pass a special resolution under section 32 of the Companies Act 1993 to amend the constitution, with the amended constitution filed with the Companies Office within 10 working days.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Filing of Form NZCN1 and Payment of Registration Fee
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Companies Register online incorporation service
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete and electronically lodge Form NZCN1 with the following particulars: proposed company name, registered office in New Zealand, address for service, full details of directors and their consents, share structure and initial allotments, and any constitution adoption statement. Pay the statutory incorporation fee of NZ$105.00 by credit card or direct debit. Upon successful processing, the Registrar issues the Certificate of Registration and the company automatically receives an NZBN.
required_dossiers: Completed Form NZCN1
Signed consent to act forms for all directors
Registered office consent form signed by the registered office provider
Evidence of payment of the incorporation fee
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar issues a requisition or query, the applicant must respond through the Companies Office online mailbox within 20 working days. The response must correct or supplement the deficient particulars. Failure to respond results in withdrawal of the application under section 15(2), in which case a fresh application and new fee will be required.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: IRD Number, GST Registration, and Employer Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Inland Revenue, New Zealand), using the integrated Companies Office application or the myIR online services portal
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Apply for the company IRD number simultaneously with incorporation through the Companies Office integrated application, or separately using form IR 596. Elect GST registration where annual taxable supplies are expected to exceed NZ$60,000, or voluntarily register to enable input credits on warehouse lease, equipment, and freight costs. Register as an employer if any New Zealand-based staff or contractors will be engaged. Obtain a unique IRD number and confirm compliance with automatic exchange of information obligations concerning controllng persons.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Registration and NZBN
IRD number application (IR 596 or online equivalent)
GST registration election with forecast turnover figures
Bank account details for the company
Director and ultimate beneficial owner information for CRS/FATCA purposes
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If Inland Revenue queries the application, the representative must correct any mismatched director or beneficial owner data through the myIR portal or by resubmitting form IR 342. Tax registration is effective from the date of application upon cure, and any late registration penalties may be remitted if reasonable cause is demonstrated.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First Board Meeting, Statutory Registers, and Share Certificates
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of directors of the company and the appointed corporate services agent
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the first board meeting, whether physically in New Zealand or by virtual meeting in accordance with the constitution. Present and adopt the pro forma First Board Resolution covering share subscription and allotment, adoption of the registered office and address for service, and appointment of directors and officers. Issue share certificates to subscribers. Establish the statutory registers including the register of members under section 87, the register of directors under section 148, and the minute book under section 189. Authorise opening of bank accounts and execution of commercial leases.
required_dossiers: First board meeting minutes or written resolution
Share certificates executed under board authority
Register of members and register of directors
Bank mandate and account opening forms
Registered office service agreement
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Where a procedural defect is found in the allotment or appointment process, the board may ratify the action by a subsequent board or shareholder resolution, and any correction to the Companies Register must be lodged using the online change of company details service with the applicable fee.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Warehouse Premises Compliance and Occupational Health and Safety Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Local territorial authority (city or district council), WorkSafe New Zealand, and Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Secure the cross-dock warehouse premises by lease or ownership. Obtain a building warrant of fitness (BWOF) from the territorial authority where the building has a compliance schedule, including annual inspections by an Independent Qualified Person (IQP) for fire suppression, emergency lighting, and mechanical systems. Submit a fire evacuation scheme to Fire and Emergency New Zealand where the facility has more than 10 employees. Establish a written health and safety policy and worker participation system under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, identify notifiable events, and notify WorkSafe if any high-hazard activities such as on-site generation or refrigerant storage are introduced.
required_dossiers: Lease agreement or certificate of title for the warehouse
Building warrant of fitness and compliance schedule
Fire evacuation scheme approved by FENZ
Independent Qualified Person inspection reports
Health and safety policy, hazard register, and emergency response plan
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: In case of a compliance defect notice from the council or WorkSafe, the company must submit a corrective action plan within the specified deadline, engage licensed professionals to rectify structural, fire, or safety deficiencies, and request re-inspection. Failure to cure within the statutory period may result in infringement fees, which can be appealed to the District Court.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: No dedicated industrial licensing board exists for ISIC 5210 warehousing and storage activities in New Zealand. Regulatory competency is distributed among the local territorial authority for building and land-use consent, WorkSafe New Zealand for occupational health and safety, and the Environmental Protection Authority together with the regional unitary council for environmental and discharge regulation.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: No statutory operating licence applies to cross-dock warehouse and third-party logistics fulfillment services under New Zealand law. The company must instead maintain a Building Warrant of Fitness under the Building Act 2004 where a compliance schedule exists, obtain any required resource consent or permitted activity compliance under the Resource Management Act 1991, and register as a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) with no separate licence but with statutory duties under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) for nationally significant proposals and national environmental standards; regional and unitary councils, such as Auckland Council for the Auckland Region, as consent authorities under the Resource Management Act 1991
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Permitted or Controlled Activity. A full environmental impact assessment and EPA application is generally not mandated for a standard cross-dock logistics warehouse. The activity normally requires either a permitted activity compliance certificate or a controlled land-use and discharge resource consent from the regional council where stormwater, traffic, or noise effects exceed plan thresholds.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Stormwater and wastewater discharges must comply with the applicable regional plan water quality standards and the National Environmental Standards for Sources of Drinking Water. No trade wastewater or hazardous substance discharge is permitted to municipal sewer or natural waterways without a council trade waste consent. If diesel generators or refrigeration plant are installed, emissions must comply with the National Environmental Standards for Air Quality 2004, including PM10 and NOx limits. Waste handling must follow the Waste Minimisation Act 2008 and the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act 1996, including classification, manifesting, and disposal obligations for any warehoused chemicals or lithium-ion batteries.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) approval of a fire evacuation scheme is required for warehouse premises with more than 10 employees. A Building Warrant of Fitness with annual inspections by an Independent Qualified Person is mandatory under the Building Act 2004. Structural load certification is required for racking, mezzanine floors, and heavy mechanical handling equipment. The company must maintain a compliant workplace under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, including worker engagement, a hazard register, emergency plans, and incident notification to WorkSafe New Zealand for any notifiable event within 48 hours.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Inland Revenue, Te Tari Taake) — New Zealand's national tax authority administering income tax, Goods and Services Tax (GST), and employer obligations; online portal: myIR at https://www.ird.govt.nz. Export customs administration is separately handled by the New Zealand Customs Service through the Trade Single Window (TSW) at https://www.customs.govt.nz.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign entity, including an offshore International Company (CK_IC) engaged in cross-border e-commerce fulfilment, must first determine whether it carries on a 'taxable activity' in New Zealand under section 6 of the GST Act 1985 or derives New Zealand-source income under sections YD4 to YD8 of the Income Tax Act 2007. If nexus is established, the entity must apply to Inland Revenue for an IRD number. Procedures: (i) a non-resident company not registered on the NZ Companies Register files Form IR742 (IRD number application) together with certified incorporation documents, registry extracts, and director/shareholder details; (ii) GST registration uses Form IR596 or the myIR non-resident GST workflow and is compulsory when taxable supplies made in New Zealand exceed or are expected to exceed NZD 60,000 in any 12-month period; a non-resident supplying remote services to NZ consumers must register once NZ-consumer turnover exceeds NZD 60,000, with voluntary registration available below that threshold; (iii) companies incorporated on the NZ Companies Register obtain an IRD number automatically at incorporation. A CK_IC operating a purely offshore cross-dock and overseas 3PL warehouse, with no physical presence, staff, or inventory in New Zealand, generally has no NZ tax registration obligation; the entity should maintain documentary proof that title, custody, and physical export movement occur outside New Zealand.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Tax_Exempt_Zone — In its home jurisdiction, the Cook Islands International Company (CK_IC) is ordinarily tax-exempt as an international company under the Cook Islands International Companies Act 2008-09, subject to satisfying the exempt international company attestation and having no disqualifying local shareholder categories. For New Zealand tax purposes, a non-resident tax-exempt foreign company is not automatically exempt: it is taxed only on New Zealand-source income and on income attributable to a New Zealand fixed establishment or permanent establishment. In the absence of a PE arising from pure offshore cross-dock, warehousing, or 3PL order-fulfilment activity, no NZ entity-level income tax is imposed, and the entity is treated as outside the NZ GST net. If a PE or fixed establishment in New Zealand is found, the NZ branch becomes subject to NZ corporate income tax on attributed income and the entity must register and account for GST on NZ taxable supplies.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: New Zealand has no check-the-box entity classification election. The available statutory and administrative elections relevant to a CK_IC cross-border fulfilment structure include: (1) GST grouping election under sections 55 to 55B of the GST Act 1985 for related companies to file consolidated GST returns; (2) look-through company (LTC) election for NZ-incorporated close companies under sections HB 1 to HB 11 of the Income Tax Act 2007, not available to offshore international companies; (3) branch versus subsidiary election principles for foreign companies deriving business income through a New Zealand PE, including application of the PE attribution rules under section YD5; (4) controlled foreign company (CFC) attribution elections where NZ-resident shareholders hold interests in the CK_IC; and (5) hybrid mismatch rule elections under subpart FH of the Income Tax Act 2007, which apply to cross-border hybrid arrangements involving the CK_IC and require adjustment of deductions, income inclusions, or the application of the 'taxed once' and 'deduction/no inclusion' outcomes. Any election must be made via the relevant NZ return or disclosure form in myIR within the statutory timeframes.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: New Zealand Goods and Services Tax (GST) — a broad-based value-added tax imposed under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985, including the remote services regime (subpart 8B) for non-resident suppliers of digital and cross-border services.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 (compulsory registration threshold under section 51(1)(b) of the GST Act 1985, based on actual or expected taxable supplies made in New Zealand in any 12-month period; the same NZD 60,000 threshold applies to non-resident suppliers of remote services to New Zealand consumers; a non-resident with only zero-rated export supplies and no NZ fixed establishment has no compulsory registration obligation unless it makes standard-rated supplies from goods held in a New Zealand warehouse).
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: None — New Zealand does not impose real-time fiscal clearance, mandatory digital stamping, or government API-based invoice authentication. E-invoicing is voluntary and operates through the PEPPOL network, with the New Zealand Peppol Authority hosted within Inland Revenue. GST is self-assessed and remitted via periodic returns (form IR372) submitted electronically through myIR. A seven-year statutory record-keeping obligation applies under section 22 of the Tax Administration Act 1994. Export declarations are lodged with the New Zealand Customs Service through the Trade Single Window (TSW) API/EDI platform; commercial invoices are not fiscally stamped. A 3PL cross-dock operator should nevertheless implement API-integrated inventory and export documentation systems to substantiate zero-rating claims.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Goods: a GST-registered supplier zero-rates exported goods under section 11(1)(a) of the GST Act 1985 where the goods are physically exported from New Zealand by the supplier or the supplier's agent within 28 days after the time of supply, or within any extended period allowed by the Commissioner, and the supplier retains credible evidence of export. Services: section 11A zero-rates services supplied to a non-resident person who is outside New Zealand when the services are performed, provided the services are not performed directly in connection with New Zealand land or a New Zealand-resident recipient and the economic benefit is received offshore; this covers offshore warehousing, order fulfilment, cross-dock handling, freight forwarding support, and logistics management supplied by a non-resident 3PL to overseas merchants. Remote services supplied to NZ consumers by a non-resident seller using a New Zealand fulfilment hub are standard-rated at 15% unless the goods are thereafter exported; B2B remote services supplied to a GST-registered New Zealand business may be zero-rated under the reverse-charge mechanism in section 8(4B) of the GST Act 1985.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: New Zealand Customs export declaration lodged electronically via the Trade Single Window (TSW), referencing the correct Harmonised System code, statistical value, and exporter-of-record details

Bill of Lading or Air Waybill evidencing physical export of the goods from New Zealand within the statutory 28-day zero-rating window, including vessel/flight details, port or airport of discharge, and consignee information
Inward Remittance Certificate or irrecoverable bank transfer evidence (SWIFT/MT103 or foreign-currency bank statement) evidencing receipt of the export sale consideration from the overseas buyer
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Export zero-rating claims are audited jointly by Inland Revenue and the New Zealand Customs Service. If the statutory export conditions are not genuinely satisfied, or if documentation is fabricated or materially misleading, GST becomes payable retrospectively; section 13 of the GST Act 1985 permits reassessment and recovery of the GST shortfall for the relevant taxable period, with refunds clawed back and use-of-money interest applied. Civil penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994 include shortfall penalties of 20% for failure to take reasonable care or for an unacceptable tax position, 100% for an abusive tax position, and 150% for evasion under section 141, in addition to criminal prosecution under sections 143A and 143B with fines up to NZD 50,000 for a first offence and imprisonment of up to five years for evasion. Director and officer personal liability may arise. False export declarations may also constitute offences under the Customs and Excise Act 2018 and the Crimes Act 1961. A deliberate contrivance using a tax-exempt offshore entity to claim zero-rating without underlying physical exports is vulnerable to general anti-avoidance recharacterisation under sections BG 1 and GA 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007, and to Inland Revenue's controlled foreign company and hybrid mismatch rules.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ; Māori: Te Pūtea Matua) — sole central bank and prudential supervisor of registered banks, with the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) jointly regulating capital-market conduct and the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) registering and supervising non-bank money-service businesses and EMI providers under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand operates a fully convertible, free-float currency regime. There are no exchange-control laws, no requirement for central-bank approval on current-account or capital-account transactions, and no foreign-exchange allocation quotas. Profit remittance (dividends, interest, royalties) by the International Company (IC) to non-resident beneficiaries is unrestricted and limited only by the general non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) obligations under New Zealand tax law; no FX visa, no capital-export licensing, and no prior notification to RBNZ is required for ordinary trade remittances. The only administrative touch-points are (i) RBNZ Balance of Payments / International Investment Position (BoP/IIP) statistical reporting for external borrowings exceeding NZ$1 million, and (ii) Overseas Investment Office (OIO) screening for 'sensitive land' or 'significant business assets' — neither of which constrains the cross-dock e-commerce fulfilment treasury flows. Within the IC's Tax-Exempt-Zone classification, tax gross-up and NRWT neutralisation must be evidenced by an IRD tax-residency certificate and the applicable double-tax-agreement election before the first distribution.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. New Zealand imposes no statutory timeline and no mandatory conversion ratio for export receipts. The IC may retain 100% of export proceeds in free-balance foreign currency (USD, CNY, EUR, AUD) held in offshore or onshore accounts, convert to NZD at any time at market rates, or deploy those proceeds directly to fund overseas fulfilment-centre inventory. No centralised export liquidation or repatriation certificate is required. For customs and statistical purposes only, export entries must be reported through the New Zealand Customs Service Electronic Single Window (ESW) with the applicable working-code tariff classification aligned to ISIC 5210 / NAICS 493110, but this does not trigger any FX surrender obligation.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Capital Escrow Account / Cross-Border RMB Clearing Account (alternative corridor for APAC settlement)

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility Rating: High (for operational FX, mass payouts and collection) / Medium (for statutory capital escrow where a licensed bank is mandatory). Airwallex (New Zealand) Limited is a registered financial-services provider and DIA-supervised money remitter under the AML/CFT Act 2009, fully authorised to run multi-currency global accounts, local ACH rails, and MT103/SWIFT payment corridors for the IC's cross-dock 3PL disbursements; Wise N.Z. Limited is additionally viable for low-ticket seller-proceeds payouts. Legal constraints: (i) EMIs in New Zealand are not 'registered banks' and cannot take custodial deposits in the statutory sense — a Capital Escrow Account housing shareholder equity must be held at an RBNZ-registered bank to preserve clean segregation and audit output; (ii) EMIs cannot issue Commercial Letters of Credit or provide UCP600 trade-finance instruments; (iii) EMI settlement into FX-constrained jurisdictions (e.g., China) requires the EMI to operate through local licensed partners, so the IC should retain a SWIFT-anchor bank for high-value settlements. Recommended structure: Tier-1 registered bank for escrow/LC/trade core plus Airwallex for last-mile fulfilment, supplier payout, and marketplace collections across 60+ markets.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: No statutory physical-presence requirement. Under the AML/CFT Act 2009 and the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism (Definitions) Regulations 2011, reporting entities may complete Customer Due Diligence (CDD) via secure electronic identity verification (EIV) — including ICAO e-Passport NFC checks, Equifax or NZ Post RealMe verification, and recorded video-conference interviews — for a low-risk-standard e-commerce fulfilment entity. In practice, ANZ, BNZ and ASB permit fully remote corporate onboarding for the IC if the director/UBO completes a 20-minute video identification, supplies the certified passport biometric data page, and confirms the registered-office address through the NZ Companies Office extract. Kiwibank and Bank of China (New Zealand) may occasionally request a single in-person meeting with the principal officer via their representative office; remote-video waivers are routinely granted for directors domiciled in Australia, Singapore, Hong Kong and the United Kingdom. Conclusion: physical travel to Auckland or Christchurch is not mandated, but keeping the managing director available for one video-interview window materially increases Tier-1 approval probability.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Opaque beneficial-ownership structure of the IC (Tax-Exempt-Zone trust wrapper concealing ultimate controllers).
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified copy of the Certificate of Incorporation; current NZ Companies Office extract listing shareholders and reserve powers; full register of members and beneficial owners; the underlying trust deed or IC constitutional document with a signed settlor structure chart; ICAO biometric passports of every UBO holding an economic threshold above 25%; and an independent legal opinion confirming the non-resident ownership chain.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Tax-exempt characterisation flagged as a potential shell or conduit vehicle lacking commercial substance.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Local-counsel tax-classification opinion demonstrating the IC's Tax-Exempt-Zone compliance; IRD non-resident tax-status certificate and non-resident asset declaration; two-year audited or reviewed financial statements; an exclusive cross-dock warehouse lease or master 3PL service agreement within ISIC 5210 / NAICS 493110; payroll and HR records evidencing actual operational headcount; platform fulfilment contracts with marketplaces; and operational evidence (gate-movement logs, inventory scans) confirming real logistics activity.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cross-border e-commerce revenue projections inconsistent with the IC's declared balance-sheet size and the overseas-warehouse proposal.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Business-model narrative and 24-month pro-forma profit-and-loss statement with conservative tri-case scenarios; signed supplier purchase orders and overseas-warehouse service agreements; marketplace seller-dashboard statements; a forecast intercompany settlement schedule; and a funds-flow memorandum explaining the entry of capital into New Zealand and onward trade disbursement.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Foreign director and absence of a physical New Zealand office.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Engagement letter of the NZ-registered agent; virtual-office lease and registered-office address evidence; directors' residential proofs (photographic ID and utility bill dated within three months); where applicable, appointment of a local alternate director; and the company's written undertaking to notify the bank of any director change under section 86 of the Companies Act 1993.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Source-of-wealth concerns where capital injection originates from a non-common-law high-friction jurisdiction or a family trust outside FATF-recognised systems.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Original SWIFT ordering-bank statements for the injected funds; contractual chain-of-title (sale, redemption or loan agreements); tax clearances from the origin jurisdiction; FATF jurisdictional confirmation; completed source-of-wealth questionnaire; and a signed cash-flow path diagram executed by external counsel showing the complete string from origin to final beneficial account.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Protocol: (1) The overseas parent or trust makes a SWIFT MT103/MT202 remittance to the IC's RBNZ-authorised bank account using a contemporaneous payment narrative: 'Equity injection under Companies Act 1993 — IC treasury — Tax-Exempt structure — working capital for ISIC 5210 cross-dock operations'. (2) The beneficiary bank maps the credit internally to RBNZ BoP/IIP statistical category 'Direct Investment — Equity Capital'; no prior FX licence is required, but the bank will obtain the UBO KYC pack and the IC board resolution authorising the account before accepting the first credit. (3) For capital-escrow treatment, direct the funds into a designated interest-bearing Capital Escrow sub-ledger, with a client-moneys / trust-account confirmation under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 where applicable; nominal share capital and shareholder advances must respectively be supported by a share-register entry and a formal loan agreement. (4) If the contribution crosses the OIO 'significant business assets' threshold (approximately NZ$100 million for non-partner-country investors and higher for partner-country investors, being Australia and the United States) or involves 'sensitive land', obtain a prior OIO consent certificate under the Overseas Investment Act 2005 before the wire exits the clearing system; for this fulfilment-hub model, the threshold review is typically not triggered because the domestic asset value remains far below the statutory cap. (5) Within five business days of receipt, the bank issues the advising receipt, SWIFT acknowledgment, and daily availability confirmation in the IC's treasury view; a one-off internal audit file is retained containing the source-of-funds trail, the board resolution and the exact purpose-code mapping.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Clearing rails are tiered by value and counterparty jurisdiction: (i) SWIFT MT103 (cover MT202/MT202COV) direct-pay protocol for high-value inventory procurement and overseas-warehouse rents, executed through the Tier-1 bank with SWIFT GPI cross-border tracking and FX Global Code compliant execution; (ii) UCP600-compliant Commercial Letters of Credit — issued as sight or usance LCs via the IC's New Zealand bank through SWIFT MT700/MT701 and confirmed, where necessary, through a Hong Kong or Singapore confirming house — for large consignment purchases from APAC manufacturers, using MT707 for amendments and MT754 with the shipping-document drawdown package for payment; (iii) local ACH rails (via Airwallex or Wise) for high-frequency low-value disbursements to supplier networks, cross-dock labour, courier tariffs and marketplace payouts in 60+ jurisdictions (United States via ACH/RTP/CHIPS, Eurozone via SEPA Instant, United Kingdom via FPS, Australia and New Zealand via BECS/PayTo, Singapore via FAST), with IC treasury retaining a nostro buffer in each settlement corridor; and (iv) USD/EUR clean collections for third-party logistics-warehouse charges where no LC was drawn. A settlement policy of gross payments above USD 250,000 requiring SWIFT MT103, amounts between USD 5,000 and USD 250,000 being local-ACH optimised, and amounts below USD 5,000 being batched, is recommended to minimise transaction leakage.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX Forwards (outright or window) between NZD and USD, CNY, EUR and AUD — fully permissible without RBNZ approval, available from one-week to twelve-month tenors under standard ISDA/CSA or bank master agreements for the IC as a wholesale eligible investor.
FX Swaps (including overnight index swaps and single-currency overnight rollovers) — permitted for managing short-dated funding and rolling cross-dock nostro buffers without creating open FX risk.

Cross-Currency Swaps (NZD/USD) — permissible where the IC's escrow is funded in NZD but trade payables are USD or CNY denominated, executing a medium-tenor principal-and-interest exchange with a licensed bank or derivatives dealer.

FX Options (plain-vanilla calls and puts) — permissible as over-the-counter hedging instruments under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 wholesale-investor exemption, enabling a contractual ceiling on procurement-currency movements while retaining downside gain if the NZD strengthens.

Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) — permissible only for the non-convertible or exotic underlying leg (e.g., CNY, IDR, INR) where the NZD or USD leg is deliverable; for a plain NZD/USD hedge a deliverable forward is the default instrument, and a purely NZD-on-NZD NDF would not be recognised as ordinary hedging since the NZD is fully convertible.
Listed NZD/USD Futures on ASX — permissible and exchange-traded for high-visibility treasury positions, although OTC forwards normally provide better tenor alignment with the fulfilment pipeline.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return comprising updated registered office details, registered agent, director particulars, shareholding structure, and shareholder confirmation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within one month after the anniversary of incorporation; early filing permitted in the month preceding the annual return date
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing fee of NZ$237.40 (approximately USD 145) applied per lodgement; Companies Office reminder notices issued; two consecutive years of non-filing triggers administrative strike-off and dissolution under the Companies Act 1993

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual confirmation and maintenance of statutory registers, including share transfer updates, director changes, and registered office records
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporate records maintained at the New Zealand registered office; no separate filing unless a change notice or shareholder resolution is lodged
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Ongoing obligation; each share transfer must be entered in the Register of Members within one month of lodging the instrument of transfer; annual review to be completed no later than the annual return date
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Defective or missing statutory registers constitute an offence under the Companies Act 1993; directors exposed to fines up to NZ$50,000; persistent non-compliance supports Registrar-initiated removal from the register

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Financial statements and annual audit determination (audit exemption certificate or audited financial statements) for the preceding balance date
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office for lodgement; independent auditor licensed under the Auditor Regulation Act 2011 for audit engagement
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Financial statements must be completed within five months of balance date; filed with the Companies Office within 20 working days of completion where the entity is not exempt; balance date typically 31 March
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to complete or file financial statements under the Financial Reporting Act 2013 may attract fines up to NZ$50,000 and continuing daily penalties; repeated non-compliance is a trigger for administrative strike-off

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Independent audit is mandatory where the entity is a 'large' company under the Financial Reporting Act 2013 (total revenue exceeding NZ$30 million, total assets exceeding NZ$60 million, or 50 or more full-time equivalent employees), or where the company is an FMC reporting entity, or a shareholder holding at least 5% of voting rights validly requires an audit; entities below these thresholds may rely on an audit exemption certificate
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: New Zealand IFRS; eligible small and medium companies may apply NZ IFRS Reduced Disclosure Regime, and non-reporting entities may use Tier 3 simplified reporting requirements

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: New Zealand does not maintain a separate public UBO register for International Company entities; the annual return declaration confirms current shareholders and directors, and the Register of Members is the authoritative ownership record. Every share transfer must be registered within one month with the transferor and transferee particulars; the annual return is certified as true and correct, and beneficial ownership information is preserved in corporate records at the registered office.

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No general tax holidays or preferential CIT rate; the 28% rate is flat. New Zealand operates a full imputation system, allowing attached imputation credits to resident shareholders. Specific concessions potentially relevant to an overseas 3PL operator include R&D tax credits (15% on eligible R&D), the approved income equalisation scheme for primary producers, and loss continuity rules under the shareholder continuity and business continuity tests. No special regime exists for cross-dock warehouse or logistics activities.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 Company Income Tax Return, filed electronically via Inland Revenue's myIR portal or approved tax software; IR4J supplementary return (transfer pricing and cross-border related-party transactions) and IR4S (international tax schedule) are attached where applicable. Companies with imputation accounts must also file an imputation return (IR4J part or separate IR4J imputation schedule).
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: For a standard 31 March balance date, the IR4 return is due 7 July following the end of the income year (or 7 April of the following year for certain taxpayers if an extension applies? Standard terminal tax and filing date is 7 July for non-provisional taxpayers? Actually, for most companies, due date is 7 July after balance date if filing electronically, and terminal tax payment is due 7 April? I must be precise: The standard due date for a company's income tax return is 7 July following the balance date. However, if the company has a non-standard balance date, the due date is the last day of the seventh month after balance date. The terminal tax due date is 7 April for a 31 March balance date. I will phrase: 'For a 31 March balance date, IR4 is due 7 July; terminal tax due 7 April. For non-standard balance dates, due dates align to the corresponding month. Provisional tax instalments generally due 28 August, 15 January and 7 May.'

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Assessable income less allowable deductions from all New Zealand-sourced business activities, including cross-dock fulfilment fees, storage charges, and ancillary services.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident companies must include only New Zealand-sourced income. If the company has a fixed place of business in New Zealand (e.g., a cross-dock warehouse), it is subject to net basis assessment on attributable profits.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Credits attached to dividends received, imputation account opening and closing balances, and imputation ratio calculations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-residents are generally not entitled to imputation credits on dividends received unless credits are attached under a special election; enter credits only where a valid imputation election exists.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 3 / IR4: Tax losses carried forward
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Prior-year net losses claimed under shareholder continuity or business continuity tests.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident-owned companies must trace shareholding continuity through the top New Zealand resident shareholders to utilise losses; if continuity is broken, losses are forfeited.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Disclosure of cross-border related-party transactions, allocation methodologies, comparability factors, and arm's length outcome.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A 3PL cross-dock operator must detail management fees, logistics service charges, intercompany loans, and any New Zealand-outbound charges to related foreign parties.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Interest paid to non-residents, deemed interest on worldwide debt arrangements, offshore branch income, and controlled foreign company interests.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident 3PL entities with New Zealand loans must complete the IFA schedule and confirm arm's length interest and thin capitalisation compliance.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty of NZ$250 per month for small taxpayers and NZ$500 per month for non-small taxpayers, continuing until the return is filed, capped at six months' worth as an initial penalty but additional monthly penalties may accrue for repeated non-filing. Late payment penalties: 1% of unpaid tax per month, plus use-of-money interest on the outstanding tax (currently above 8.5% per annum).

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: The statutory non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) on dividends is 15%. Under many double tax agreements (DTAs), the rate may be reduced to 5% (or 0% for substantial shareholdings, typically 80% or more, depending on the treaty). New Zealand's imputation system does not override NRWT on non-resident recipients.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke DTA relief, the non-resident dividend recipient must provide the New Zealand payer with a valid tax residence certificate issued by the tax authority of the treaty country, usually accompanied by a completed Inland Revenue declaration (e.g., IR290 or specific treaty form) certifying beneficial ownership and entitlement to the reduced rate. The payer must accept and retain the certificate before making payment, failing which the statutory NRWT must be withheld. Retroactive treaty rate claims can be made by filing an NRWT refund application within the relevant time bar (generally four years from the end of the tax year). For interest and royalties, similar DTA certificate requirements apply.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Royalties: statutory NRWT is 15%; under most New Zealand DTAs the rate is reduced to 10% or 5% depending on the treaty and type of IP. Interest: statutory NRWT is 15%; under many DTAs the rate is reduced to 10%, with 0% for certain government or approved financial institution interest. Additionally, the approved issuer levy (AIL) of 2% may apply to qualifying related-party interest paid to non-residents if the lender is a non-resident and the borrower is a New Zealand resident company, and the interest is not otherwise subject to NRWT (subject to conditions and anti-avoidance rules).

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: New Zealand's transfer pricing documentation threshold is NZ$10 million in aggregate cross-border related-party transactions per income year. Where the aggregate value of transactions covered by the transfer pricing rules exceeds NZ$10 million, the taxpayer is expected to prepare and maintain contemporaneous documentation, including a Master File and Local File consistent with OECD guidance, and to file the IR4J transfer pricing disclosure schedule.
approved_arm_length_methodologies: CUP, Resale Price, Cost Plus, TNMM, Profit Split
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not have a separate 'Economic Substance Regulations' code (e.g., as in CARICOM-style regimes), but the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) under section BG 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007, prior case law (e.g., Peterson, Ben Nevis Forestry), and the anti-conduit provisions require that an entity possess real commercial substance. A cross-dock 3PL entity must maintain genuine physical presence in New Zealand for the warehouse operation, assume operational risks, employ staff or engage real service providers, and perform substantive logistics functions. An entity used merely as an invoicing hub with no actual warehousing or fulfilment activity is not recognised for tax purposes and risks reconstruction.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to return New Zealand-sourced income arising from cross-dock warehousing and fulfilment operations, such as storage fees, handling fees, or management fees received from New Zealand customers; deliberately creating false invoices or omitting substantial revenue streams.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under Tax Administration Act 1994 (TAA) sections 141B and 143, evasion may attract a shortfall penalty of up to 150% of the evaded tax, a fine on conviction of up to NZ$250,000 (individual) or NZ$500,000 (company), and imprisonment for up to four years (section 143B).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and senior officers who knowingly participate in or direct the evasion may be held criminally liable; under TAA section 149A, a director may be personally liable for company tax debts and penalties when the company has failed to pay and the director knew or should have known of the unpaid tax, or when assets are stripped to defeat Inland Revenue collection. Travel bans and asset restraint orders may be imposed under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Setting cross-border related-party charges for warehouse storage, cross-docking, shipment handling, or logistics management substantially below or above arm's length prices; failing to keep contemporaneous documentation where aggregate related-party transactions exceed NZ$10 million; not filing IR4J disclosure.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Inland Revenue may adjust the taxable income to the arm's length consideration under the Income Tax Act 2007 sections GC 6-GC 8. Shortfall penalties apply: 20% for an unacceptable tax position, 40% for lack of reasonable care, or 150% for fraudulent avoidance; documentation penalty of up to NZ$20,000 may be imposed for failure to maintain required transfer pricing records under TAA section 141FB.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be personally liable for the company's tax liabilities and transfer pricing penalties if they were knowingly party to the non-compliance, failed to ensure the company made adequate tax provision, or permitted the company to enter into a tax avoidance transaction that strips the company of assets.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating the International Company as a letterbox entity with no actual employees, warehouse functions, or business activity in New Zealand, using artificial contracts to book profits offshore, or engaging in circular intercompany transactions solely to obtain tax advantages.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Section BG 1 GAAR allows Inland Revenue to nullify the tax advantage, reconstruct the arrangement, and impose shortfall penalties up to 100% of the resulting tax shortfall. The Companies Office may deregister the company for not carrying on business, which dissolves the entity and removes limited liability protection; also, director disqualification under the Companies Act 1993 may apply.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: The corporate veil may be pierced where the company is a sham or facade; directors may be personally liable for unpaid company taxes and to creditors for fraudulent trading under section 301 of the Companies Act 1993 (if the business was carried on with intent to defraud creditors), and may face imprisonment for perjury if false declarations are made to Inland Revenue or the Companies Office.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML / CFT and Money Laundering Breaches
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using the 3PL cross-dock operation to facilitate money laundering via undetected payments on Airwallex platforms, local ACH rails, or wire transfers; accepting funds from illegal e-commerce activities; failing to perform customer due diligence; or intentionally structuring payments to avoid AML thresholds.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, a reporting entity may face a civil penalty of up to NZ$2.5 million for the first breach and up to NZ$5 million for a subsequent or continued breach, plus infringement notices. Criminal money laundering offences under the Crimes Act 1961 carry imprisonment of up to seven years per offence; property obtained through significant criminal activity may be forfeited under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and senior managers who directed, participated in, or facilitated AML/CFT non-compliance are individually liable, with penalties up to NZ$100,000 per individual per offence; they may be disqualified from managing companies. A director convicted of money laundering can be sentenced to imprisonment and prohibited from holding directorships under the Companies Act 1993.
